easy.heading: Warming Up With a Monday Morning Treat
easy.body:
Starting my week with the easy puzzle was like having a nice warm muffin with my coffee. The first thing I noticed were those equals regions. When you see cells like 1,0 and 1,1 being marked as equal to their neighbors, it really helps narrow down where the dominoes can sit. I started by looking at the sum constraint of 1 at cell 0,3. Since the cell at 1,3 was marked as empty, I knew the 1,3 domino had to fit right there. It was the only way to get a total of 1 while using a domino that could bridge into an empty spot.

After that, the rest of the board started to fall into place. I used the equals constraints at 2,0 and 2,1 to place another piece. The trickiest part was making sure I didn't mix up my dominoes, like the 5,4 and the 1,5. By looking at the equals constraint between 2,2 and 2,3, I realized I needed the 5,4 domino there because it was the only one left that could satisfy the high value needed for the other sections. It was a really satisfying solve that took less time than brewing my second cup of joe!

medium.heading: Midday Magic With Some Heavy Totals
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today felt like a little step up, mostly because of those big sum targets. Seeing a target of 10 at 0,2 and 1,2 really made me pause. I had to look at my remaining dominoes like the 6,6 and the 5,3 to see what could possibly add up. I eventually realized that the domino at 1,2 and 1,3 had to be part of that sum. By pairing the 3,3 domino at 3,3 and 3,4, where 3,4 is an empty cell, I managed to clear out a lot of the bottom half of the grid.

I struggled for a minute with the sum of 5 at cells 3,0 and 3,1. I initially thought about using a 2 and 3, but looking at my available dominoes, the 4,1 piece was the perfect fit. Once that was set, I could see that the 2,1 and 2,2 sum of 2 was going to be easy to finish. I placed the 5,1 domino across 1,1 and 2,1, which meant the 1 in the 2,1 spot was exactly what I needed to help reach that sum of 2. It was all about finding that one anchor point and building out from there.

hard.heading: The Big Finale To Wrap Up The Day
hard.body:
Wow, the hard puzzle today was a real brain teaser! The biggest challenge was definitely the massive sum of 16 down at 7,2, 8,2, and 9,2. With dominoes only going up to 6, you know you need some heavy hitters there. I spent a long time looking at the 6,4 and 6,2 dominoes. When I realized the 6,2 and 8,2/9,2 dominoes had to work together, everything started to click. The breakthrough came when I spotted the empty cell at 5,6. It acted as a zero, which made the sum of 10 at 5,7 and 6,7 much easier to figure out because it had to involve the 6,4 domino.

I almost hit a dead end near the top left corner with the sum of 3 across 1,0, 1,1, and 1,2. I had to carefully count my remaining pips to see if I should use the 0,1 or the 1,2 domino. Eventually, I saw that the 1,2 domino fit perfectly at 1,2 and 0,2 to satisfy the sum of 6 at 0,2. It's like a big jigsaw puzzle where every piece only has one home. Finishing that last sum of 4 at 7,7 felt like winning a marathon. I definitely needed a refill on my coffee after this one!

explanation.tips: Try to look for regions with a sum of zero or one first, as they have very few possible combinations. Also, keep an eye on empty cells because they usually count as zero pips and can be a huge help in solving adjacent sums. If you get stuck, count how many times a certain number appears in your domino list to see where it must go.
explanation.learned: I learned that large sums are actually easier to solve than medium ones because they force you to use your biggest dominoes like the 6,6 or 5,5 right away. It was also interesting to see how empty cells can be used as a bridge to satisfy a sum constraint without adding any value to it.

faqs.question: What do the empty regions mean in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: Empty regions are cells that contain zero pips. They are often used to help satisfy low sum constraints or to act as a placeholder for one side of a domino.

faqs.question: Can I reuse dominoes in the same Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: No, each domino listed in the puzzle data can only be used once. Once you place the 6,4 domino, for example, you have to use different pieces for the rest of the board.

faqs.question: How do equals constraints work in Pips?
faqs.answer: An equals constraint means that the number of pips in each cell within that colored region must be the same. If the region covers three cells, all three must have the same value.

faqs.question: What is the best way to start a hard Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Start by looking for the largest and smallest sum targets. A very high sum like 16 or a very low sum like 1 often only has one or two possible domino combinations.

faqs.question: Do dominoes have to be placed vertically or horizontally?
faqs.answer: Dominoes can be placed either way! The solution will show them connecting two adjacent cells either side-by-side or one above the other.
